title: Leadership Jolein Burn the Ladder
author: Jolein
summary: Jolein, a district-level education leader, argues that the conventional career ladder in education -- from teacher to coach to assistant principal to principal to district leader -- is a dangerous mental model that equates upward movement with advancement and proximity to students with regression. The piece opens with the author's own admission that after years away from school buildings, they had lost sharpness -- and instead of hiding from it, they increased their reps (covering schools, being present in buildings). The core concept is 'muscular humility' (Daniel Coyle): a leadership posture that finds simple ways to serve the group and signals 'we are all in this together,' insisting 'I am not above practicing.' The ladder makes leaders brittle: when identity is tied only to one role or salary band, any disruption becomes existential, producing leaders who protect their image rather than tell the truth. The essay calls for leaders to build identities that work across roles -- to find worth in the work itself rather than in the title.
points: * The career ladder in education is a lie: treating every move away from students as advancement and every move closer as regression creates leaders who are brittle, image-protecting, and unable to say what is actually happening in schools. * Muscular humility (Coyle) is the leadership posture of finding simple ways to serve the group and demonstrating 'I am not above practicing' -- a direct counter to the identity trap that says senior leaders should be insulated from the daily work. * Leaders who identify primarily with a title, office, or salary band become easier to threaten, not harder; and threatened people protect their image rather than becoming more honest -- exactly the opposite of what schools need from their leaders. * The ability to jump in seamlessly is not the test of a good district leader; knowing what you don't know, asking where things are, and being willing to be seen learning is more valuable than the illusion of always having the answer. * Careers in education leadership were never meant to be linear; leaders who build their identity only for one version of importance make themselves fragile precisely because schools are not stable enough to support that kind of permanence.
quotes: I think one of the most dangerous things that can happen in education is becoming too important to practice. I mean really practice -- covering lunch duty, walking a kid back from the edge of a meltdown, or just helping a first-year teacher survive sixth hour.

Someone gave me feedback that has followed me ever since. She said I demonstrated what Daniel Coyle calls 'muscular humility.' Coyle uses that phrase to describe a leadership posture that looks for simple ways to serve the group and send the signal: we are all in this together.
Every move away from students is treated as advancement. Every move closer to students is treated as regression.
The ladder does something dangerous to our imagination. It makes movement feel like failure unless the movement is upward.

When your identity only works in one role, one salary band, one version of importance, you do not become more secure. You become easier to threaten. And threatened people do not usually become more honest. They protect their title, their image, and the illusion that they still know what is happening.

But schools are not stable enough for that lie anymore. Roles shift. Budgets collapse. Superintendents leave. Grant funding dries up. And still, somehow, we keep acting like permanence is the prize. But permanence can make us brittle.
